summary: Introduces the IOAM Direct Export (DEX) option type for in situ OAM. Rather than carrying telemetry data inside packets, the option triggers the data to be exported directly from network nodes for collection. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Instead of packets carrying notes all the way along, each stop mails its notes straight to the office. The packet just carries the signal to do that.

questions: how does ioam export telemetry data
what is the ioam dex option type
how does dex avoid overloading collectors
what is the flow id in ioam dex
subtitle: A trigger option that tells IOAM nodes to export or collect telemetry on the spot, instead of stuffing it into the packet.

tldr.problem: In situ OAM normally pushes telemetry data into packets as they travel, which makes packets grow along the path. Operators sometimes want the data to leave the packet right away instead.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9326 defines the IOAM Direct Export (DEX) Option-Type. An encapsulating node adds it to selected packets, and the nodes that see it collect and/or export the requested IOAM data without writing it into the packet.
tldr.outcome: Direct export adds a trigger that can cause every node on a path to emit data, so the RFC requires selective use and rate limiting to avoid overloading the network or the receiving entity. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9326 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2022, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9197, which defines the other IOAM option types.

sections.title: Why Direct Export
sections.content:
IOAM (In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance), defined in RFC 9197, is used for monitoring traffic and for incorporating IOAM data fields into in-flight data packets. RFC 9197 defines four IOAM-Option-Types: Pre-allocated Trace, Incremental Trace, Proof of Transit and Edge-to-Edge.

RFC 9326 adds a fifth, the IOAM Direct Export (DEX) Option-Type. It is used as a trigger for IOAM nodes to locally aggregate and process IOAM data and/or to export it to a receiving entity. A receiving entity is something inside the IOAM domain such as a collector, analyzer, controller, decapsulating node, or a software module in one of the IOAM nodes.

Despite the name, receiving a DEX option does not always create another packet. Some deployments might just use it to trigger local processing of OAM data, and that local processing is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: Most of the time, packets carry the notes. Direct export flips this: the packet carries only a request, and each stop sends its notes to the office on its own.

sections.title: How the Trigger Works
sections.content:
The DEX option is incorporated into data packets by an IOAM encapsulating node and removed by an IOAM decapsulating node. Transit nodes can read it but cannot modify it. Only encapsulating nodes are allowed to add the option, and an encapsulating node can also generate probe packets that carry it, either periodically or on demand. How those probes are specified is outside the RFC.

Each kind of node reacts differently:

  • The encapsulating node adds the option to packets (or a subset of them) and MAY export and/or collect the requested data immediately.
  • A transit node that processes a packet with the option MAY export and/or collect the requested data.
  • The decapsulating node MAY export and/or collect the data and MUST decapsulate the IOAM header.

The data can be aggregated locally and then pushed periodically to a receiving entity, or pulled by it on demand.
sections.eli5: The first router sticks the note on the packet, the routers in the middle read it and send their reports, and the last router peels the note off.

sections.title: The DEX Option-Type Format
sections.content:
The DEX option is at least 8 octets long. It starts with a 16-bit Namespace-ID (the IOAM namespace from RFC 9197), an 8-bit Flags field and an 8-bit Extension-Flags field. Next comes a 24-bit IOAM-Trace-Type, which says which IOAM data fields should be exported, followed by an 8-bit Reserved field that the receiver MUST ignore.

Optional fields follow, each exactly 4 octets long. A bit set to 1 in Extension-Flags says the matching optional field is present, so that field also gives the length of the option. A node that sees an unknown extension flag set to 1 MUST ignore the corresponding optional field.

Two optional fields are defined. The Flow ID is a 32-bit flow identifier set at the encapsulating node, shorter values being zero padded in the most significant bits. The Sequence Number is a 32-bit counter starting from 0 and incremented by 1 for each packet of the same flow at the encapsulating node that carries the DEX option. Combined, they let a collector correlate exported data from the same user packet.

The bit in IOAM-Trace-Type for the Checksum Complement field SHOULD be zero, because that field is meant for in-flight packet modifications and is not relevant for direct export.
sections.eli5: The note has a few boxes to fill in: which group it belongs to, what to report, and optionally a flow number and a counter so the office can match up reports about the same packet.

sections.title: Limiting the Load
sections.content:
If every packet carried the DEX option, the exported data could overload the network and the receiving entity. So an encapsulating node that supports DEX MUST be able to add the option to only a subset of the packets it forwards. The RFC points to existing selection and sampling methods, RFC 7014 and RFC 5475.

The traffic carrying a DEX option SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of the interface capacity on any interface of the encapsulating node, counting both forwarded packets and generated probes. If paths have at most M transit nodes, N should be much greater than M, because one packet can trigger up to M exported packets. With no knowledge of the topology, it is RECOMMENDED to use N>100.

Nodes that export MUST also be able to limit the rate of exported packets, which SHOULD NOT exceed 1/N of the interface capacity (again N>100 is recommended). A node MAY keep counters of packets it did not export because of the rate limit. Exporting over a path that is itself subject to direct export SHOULD be avoided, and an encapsulating node that recognizes an IOAM exported packet MUST NOT push a DEX option into it, which prevents nested exporting and loops.
sections.eli5: If every packet asked for a report, the office would drown in mail. So only a few packets carry the request, and each stop limits how many reports it sends.

sections.title: Nodes That Do Not Understand DEX
sections.content:
A transit or decapsulating node that receives an unknown IOAM-Option-Type ignores it, as RFC 9197 specifies, so nodes without DEX support simply skip the option. A decapsulating node removes the IOAM encapsulation and all its option types, including a DEX option it does not understand.

Skipping over an unknown DEX option depends on the encapsulation, which is outside the scope of the RFC. As an example, when IOAM is carried in IPv6 it sits in a Hop-by-Hop or Destination options header, so it can be skipped using the length field in that header.

The format of exported packets is also left open. The RFC only gives, as an example, an export format based on a work-in-progress document.
sections.eli5: If a router does not know what the sticky note means, it ignores it and passes the packet along, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security and Performance Concerns
sections.content:
Because DEX makes nodes send out extra data, an attacker can try to abuse it. Injecting synthetic packets with the option, or an on-path attacker adding or removing it, can overload IOAM nodes and receiving entities. Because one packet affects multiple devices along the path, the effect can be amplified. With several IOAM domains, exported packets from one domain could pass through another domain where they are subject to DEX again, and the RFC notes this recursive amplification could theoretically continue infinitely.

The mitigations are the rules above: selective use of DEX, rate limiting of exports, and not adding DEX to exported packets. In addition, any export method MUST secure the exported data to protect confidentiality and integrity. A node performing DEX export MUST send data to a pre-configured trusted receiving entity in the same IOAM domain, and MUST gain explicit consent before it starts sending.

The DEX option itself carries no IOAM data fields, so the integrity protection mechanism of a related draft does not apply to it. Its integrity can be protected by the encapsulating protocol. Like IOAM in general, DEX is assumed to run in a restricted administrative domain. The performance section adds that where exported data goes over an out-of-band network, an operator may choose to disable rate limiting.
sections.eli5: A bully could make routers send lots of reports to flood the office. So the rules say to ask for reports rarely, cap the mail each router sends, and only send to trusted offices.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated code point 4 in the IOAM Option-Type registry (from RFC 9197) for the DEX option, with the description 'Direct exporting'.

IANA also created two new registries, each with 8 flag bits and allocation by the IETF Review procedure: IOAM DEX Flags for the 8-bit Flags field, and IOAM DEX Extension-Flags for the Extension-Flags field. In the second, bit 0 (the most significant bit) means Flow ID and bit 1 means Sequence Number. Optional fields appear in the order of the enabled bits, starting from the most significant bit.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers now has an entry for this new kind of note, and two new lists keep track of the little switches inside it.

fields.name: Extension-Flags
fields.desc: Each bit set to 1 marks a 4-octet optional field.

fields.desc: MUST be ignored by the receiver.

items.title: Selective DEX
items.text: Encapsulating nodes MUST be able to add the option to only a subset of packets.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.text: Nodes that export MUST be able to limit their export rate.

items.title: No loops
items.text: Exported packets do not get a DEX option pushed into them.
